nameStory: Orange Rock Hair gets its name from its distinctive bright orange color and its hair-like, thread-shaped filaments that spread across rock surfaces. The scientific name 'aurea' means 'golden' in Latin, referring to the golden-orange hues created by carotenoid pigments - the same compounds that make carrots orange!
description: Orange Rock Hair is actually an algae, not a plant, that forms thin, fuzzy orange patches on rocks, walls, and tree bark. It appears as delicate, thread-like filaments that create velvety orange coatings wherever it grows. Though it's technically a green algae, you'd never guess it - the orange pigments completely mask the green chlorophyll underneath. These colonies can spread several inches across surfaces, creating distinctive orange 'stains' in the landscape.

idTips.label: Bright orange color
idTips.description: Vibrant orange to golden-orange coloration that looks almost artificial - like someone painted the surface with orange paint

idTips.label: Thread-like texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and velvety to the touch, made up of tiny hair-like filaments that you can see with a magnifying glass

idTips.label: Surface coating
idTips.description: Forms thin, spreading patches that coat the surface rather than growing upward - looks almost like colored dust from a distance

idTips.label: Multiple substrates
idTips.description: Grows on rocks, concrete walls, tree bark, old wood, and even moss - much more versatile than typical algae

idTips.label: No odor
idTips.description: Unlike some algae, has no noticeable smell even when wet - completely odorless when you get close

habitat: You'll find Orange Rock Hair on a surprising variety of surfaces throughout New England - from natural rock outcrops and stone walls to concrete structures, tree bark, and old wooden fences. It thrives in areas that stay somewhat moist but not constantly wet, often on north-facing surfaces or in partially shaded spots. Look for it in both urban and natural settings, from city sidewalks to forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant as moisture increases, with colonies appearing brighter orange and more noticeable as they respond to spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Most visible and colorful during humid periods, though may appear duller during very dry spells when the filaments contract.
seasonality.fall: Remains active and orange-colored, often becoming more prominent as other vegetation dies back and exposes surfaces where it grows.
seasonality.winter: Persists through winter as orange patches, though may appear less vibrant - still easily identifiable by its distinctive color and texture.

funFact: This 'plant' is actually neither plant nor fungus, but an algae that has completely abandoned water to live on dry land - it's essentially a former aquatic organism that learned to paint the terrestrial world orange!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for rust stains, orange lichen, or even spray paint vandalism on concrete surfaces. Unlike rust, it has a soft, fuzzy texture rather than a hard metallic feel, and unlike lichen, it forms thin coatings rather than crusty patches. Memory trick: if it feels velvety and looks too perfectly orange to be natural, it's probably Orange Rock Hair!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Orange Rock Hair,' this species has been widely misidentified in field guides and scientific literature, with the name incorrectly applied to many other orange algae species. Many historical records of this species in New England may actually represent different Trentepohlia species entirely.
compareHints: Orange Rock Hair is the most common and widespread Trentepohlia species in our region, while its closest relative Trentepohlia umbrina tends to be more brownish-orange rather than bright orange. Orange Rock Hair also grows on a wider variety of surfaces compared to its more substrate-specific relatives. If you see bright orange algae in New England, this is your most likely candidate.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Trentepohlia umbrina tends to be more reddish-orange compared to its relative Orange Rock Hair (Trentepohlia aurea), which is more yellow-orange or golden.
